title: Trenton's city finances and property taxes: why private investment stays away (or does not)
image_credit: Ken Lund from Reno, Nevada, USA / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0
image_caption: The New Jersey State House. State offices occupy much of downtown Trenton and pay no property tax.
summary: Trenton taxes property more heavily than any other town in Mercer County, yet it still depends on the state for about half of its main operating revenue. The reason is structural: a large part of the city's land belongs to the state, the county, schools, churches and charities and is exempt from tax, so a poor population and a small commercial base carry the cost of a capital city. High taxes, an aging water system, crime and population loss have discouraged private investors, although some private projects have gone forward. Every figure below was checked against a second, independent source, or it is marked unconfirmed.

p: Trenton's introduced budget for calendar year 2026 totals $298.4 million including grants, up from $281.3 million in 2025. Salaries and wages are the largest expense, at about $120.6 million, and debt service is about $18.2 million. The property tax for municipal purposes was budgeted at about $85.6 million, less than a third of the budget.

After the state reduced the city's aid (see below), the Council adopted an amended budget on 15 September. Unconfirmed: one report of that meeting quotes a city official giving the amended total as $315.4 million.

sources.label: Citizen Portal report of 15 Sep meeting

parts.note: The $298.4 million total and its parts come from two city documents, not from an independent source; the state approved the budget, which makes them reliable but not independently confirmed.

parts.h: 2. Dependence on the state, and state supervision
p: Trenton receives Transitional Aid, a program of the state Department of Community Affairs (DCA) for distressed cities. A city that takes it must accept state oversight of its finances under a memorandum of understanding. For 2026 the city asked for $59 million and received $57,318,832. It also receives $10 million in Capital City Aid, a payment that recognizes the state's tax-exempt presence in the capital.

The DCA cut about $1.7 million from the city's request because the introduced budget did not raise the tax levy, and it required a 2 percent levy increase as a condition of approval. Moody's estimates that four forms of state aid (Transitional Aid, ordinary state aid, Capital City Aid and a state payment in lieu of taxes) make up half of the city's main operating revenue in 2026. Moody's writes that without this support the city 'would be highly challenged to manage its budget.'

Unconfirmed: the city says a proposed addendum to the memorandum would require a tax levy increase of at least 3.5 percent in 2027 and later years. This comes from the city's own statement, as reported by one outlet. Also unconfirmed: Capital City Aid was created in 2004, reached $37.5 million in fiscal year 2008, and was eliminated in fiscal year 2011 (NJ Spotlight, 2019, only).

parts.h: 3. Property tax rates compared with neighboring towns
p: New Jersey publishes two rates. The general rate is applied to a property's assessed value to compute the bill. The effective rate adjusts for how far assessments lag behind market value, so it allows a fair comparison between towns.

In 2025 Trenton's general rate was $5.890 per $100 of assessed value and its effective rate 3.468 percent, the highest in Mercer County. The comparable effective rates were 2.690 percent in Ewing, 2.434 percent in Hamilton, 2.376 percent in Lawrence, 2.080 percent in West Windsor and 1.814 percent in Princeton. The owner of a house worth $300,000 at market value would thus pay roughly $10,400 a year in Trenton, $7,300 in Hamilton and $5,400 in Princeton (approximate figures computed from the effective rates).

Of Trenton's general rate, $3.758 went to the city itself, $1.148 to the schools and $0.878 to the county. Trenton's assessments stood at 60.13 percent of market value. The city set a municipal rate of 3.781 for 2026, an increase of about 2 percent.

sources.label: NJ Treasury, 2025 general and effective tax rates
NJ Treasury, 2025 abstract of ratables, Mercer

p: According to the city's 2025 budget document, taxable property in Trenton was assessed at $2.207 billion on 1 October 2024, while exempt property was assessed at $2.723 billion, which is 123 percent of the taxable base. Public property (state, county, city and federal) accounted for $1.804 billion of the exempt total, public schools for $238 million, churches and charities for $185 million, and other exempt property for $460 million.

Measured by land, NJ Spotlight reported in 2019 that state buildings and parking lots cover about a third of the city's roughly eight square miles, and that about half of the city is tax-exempt when courthouses, hospitals and churches are included. A Trentonian commentary in 2020 also gave the figure of more than 50 percent. A Harvard study in 2025 estimated that the city forgoes between $13.6 million and $35.3 million a year in taxes on state property and another $7.1 million on county property, and concluded that the high effective tax rate discourages development.

sources.label: City of Trenton, CY2025 user-friendly budget

parts.note: Unconfirmed: the assessed values of exempt property come only from the city's budget document. The share of land that is exempt (one third state, about half in total) is supported by two press sources but is several years old. The Harvard estimates of forgone tax are from one study.

parts.h: 5. The tax base and the last revaluation
p: Taxable property was assessed at about $2.2 billion, which the state equalizes to about $3.67 billion in market value. Residential property makes up about 60 percent of the taxable base, commercial property about 31 percent, apartments about 5 percent and industrial property under 3 percent. The last citywide revaluation took effect for the 2017 tax year, after a long period without one; assessments have since fallen to about 60 percent of market value, which is why the general rate is so much higher than the effective rate.

sources.label: Mayor Jackson statement on the revaluation

parts.note: Unconfirmed: the breakdown of the taxable base by class comes only from the city's budget document. The report that the revaluation before 2017 was in 1992 comes from one source.

p: A payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) replaces the regular property tax on a property, usually for a fixed number of years. In its 2026 budget the city expects $13.6 million in PILOT payments from the state for state property and $3.1 million in PILOT payments from commercial properties. The commercial figure is small compared with the $85.6 million raised by the regular municipal tax, which suggests that abatements have not drawn a large volume of private development into the city.
parts.note: Unconfirmed: both PILOT figures come only from the city's budget. I did not find a published list of individual abatements or their total value.

parts.h: 7. The water utility and the city's debt
p: Trenton Water Works, owned by the city, serves Trenton and parts of Hamilton, Ewing, Lawrence and Hopewell. In October 2022 the state Department of Environmental Protection placed it under an administrative order for failure to operate and maintain the system, and sent in an outside oversight contractor. In July 2025 the department told the city that the utility had experienced 'backsliding' on critical issues and shifted its role toward enforcement and capital planning.

The utility's capital plan for 2024 to 2033 totals about $763 million, including $175 million to replace about 20,000 lead service lines. In January 2026 it sought its first rate increase since 2020. Moody's writes that the city 'would have significant difficulty funding this capital plan on its own' and expects the state to pay for much of it. The city has about $210 million of long-term debt outstanding.
parts.note: Unconfirmed: the cost of $175 million and the count of 20,000 lead lines come from the utility, as quoted by NJ.com only.

p: On 1 May 2026 Moody's raised Trenton's rating one step, from Baa2 to Baa1, which is investment grade but in the lower part of that range. Moody's attributed the upgrade to 'significant support from the State of New Jersey,' not to growth in the city's own economy. It listed 'expansion of economic activity in the city sufficient to produce revenues enabling the city to be more self-sufficient' as a factor that could lead to a further upgrade.
parts.note: Unconfirmed: I found no current S&P rating for Trenton. One financial website lists an S&P rating of BBB-, but its other figures are out of date, so the S&P rating is not reported here.

p: Taxes. The effective rate is about 40 percent higher than in Hamilton and nearly double that of Princeton. For a commercial or apartment building, whose value depends on net income, this difference directly reduces what an investor can pay. The mayor himself told NJ Spotlight in 2019 that the city's tax levy 'is one of the impediments to residential and commercial redevelopment,' and the Harvard study of 2025 reached the same conclusion.

State dependence and rising levies. The state now requires the city to raise its levy each year as a condition of aid. The city's own five-year projection in its 2026 budget shows the municipal rate rising from 3.781 to 6.603 by 2031 if nothing else changes (city projection, not independently confirmed). An investor buying a building for twenty years must take that risk into account.

Poverty and population. The city has about 91,500 residents, more than it had in 2010 but far below its peak of about 128,000 in 1950 (Census history; the peak figure was not independently checked). Median household income is $52,537, and only 16.2 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, which limits the market for new retail and higher-priced housing.

Crime. Trenton's homicide rate remains among the highest of the large cities in the state, although shootings fell in 2025 along with the rest of New Jersey. Unconfirmed: the sources disagree on the 2025 count; one reports 16 homicides and another gives a rate of 15.4 per 100,000, which implies about 14.

Water and services. A utility under state order, with a capital need of three-quarters of a billion dollars, raises doubts about future water rates and reliability for any business that uses much water.

Vacant property and land assembly. The city's own sale of 28 abandoned buildings shows the scale of the vacancy problem. The city's Trenton250 master plan names fragmented sites, old industrial buildings without modern access, vacancy and crime as obstacles to redevelopment.

Schools and permits. Developers and residents often cite the public schools as a reason families leave, and the city's permitting process has been criticized; I did not find recent, checked data on either, so these are listed as reported concerns only.

Meridian Furniture, a company founded in Trenton, bought 10 acres on Enterprise Avenue from the city for $1 million in September 2026 to build a warehouse of about 220,000 square feet. Cheap land at the city's edge with highway access is where private industry has been willing to invest.
Rojo's Roastery is investing about $933,000 to reopen the former downtown Starbucks as a roastery and café, with a state agency grant of up to $493,000 (public subsidy).

Tetrabilt, a private developer, has been designated to renovate the empty downtown Marriott once the city buys it with a $4 million state grant (public subsidy). The private share of the renovation is not yet fixed by contract.
The Trenton Ironhawks, a privately owned professional hockey team, begin play in October 2026 at the county-owned arena.

An office-to-apartment conversion of the 16-story tower at 240 West State Street was announced by a private developer, Astoria Housing Partners, with completion targeted for 2026. Unconfirmed: I could not find its current status, and state housing records list it as a project using low-income housing tax credits (public subsidy).

Taken together, the pattern is that private money comes when the government first removes part of the cost (free or cheap land, a grant, a building bought with state money) or when the investment does not depend on the city's residents (a warehouse, a regional sports team).
